title: Eating bugs, secret to getting jacked?
summary: NH examines insect protein: nutritionally a valid but unremarkable protein source once cooking losses, taste and bioavailability hype are accounted for. He then argues insect farming is just the next stage of industrial farming, with welfare and parasite problems, and that the media push is consumerist hype dressed in morality rather than real ecology, which would mean cutting food waste and returning to permaculture.
claims: 100 g of insects gives 9 to 35 g of protein versus 16 to 20 g for meat; insects vary far more, so only a few species (crickets, worms, grasshoppers) are worth eating

claims.protein: 9-35 g/100 g insects vs 16-20 g/100 g meat

claims: Protein per 100 g is misleading for insects because you need a mountain of them to match a small piece of chicken or beef; compare foods at the same scale
Bioavailability makes or breaks a protein source; whey is popular because it is close to 100% absorbable, while many plant proteins are poorly absorbed and need more food volume
A study claiming cricket powder is 50% more digestible than whey mostly showed faster absorption, not better overall protein
When every outlet (Adidas, Men's Health, GQ) says the same thing about a product, be suspicious; bioavailability figures are largely a sales argument and some whey brands even claim 150%

Taste is the most overlooked factor: food that tastes bad will not be eaten no matter its nutrient profile; insects have no fat, an exoskeleton and little or bad flavour, which is why snacks are covered in artificial flavours
Nutrition data on raw insects is useless because nobody eats them raw; brief boiling cut insect protein bioavailability by about 25%, bringing it to roughly 60%
Roasting insects preserves protein better than boiling, but iron and zinc lost nearly 50% of their bioavailability even with roasting
Cooking meat tends to raise protein and amino acid bioavailability, so once both are compared cooked, insects and meat end up roughly equivalent protein sources
Insect promoters lead with protein as an entry argument to a protein-obsessed audience, then switch to morality and sustainability: the same one-two punch vegans use
The UN says insects need six times less feed than cattle, but about 86% of cattle feed is agricultural by-products inedible to humans, so the comparison is disingenuous
Livestock's roughly 40% share of greenhouse gases includes transport; cattle belching itself is about 3% of yearly US emissions, and insects also have to be transported and cooked
Transport accounts for about 27% of global emissions and the Netherlands imports around 70% of its insects, so insects are not emission-free in practice
It takes about 2 kg of feed to make 1 kg of insects versus 8 kg for 1 kg of beef, and about 80% of a farmed insect is eaten versus 40-60% of poultry or cattle: a real advantage for insects
Cricket powder could cost about a quarter of the price of whey once production scales
He says he would rather starve than eat a roach
Permaculture (animals and crops on the same land, e.g. chickens in a corn field eating pests and fertilising soil) is an old sustainable alternative that industrial agriculture abandoned
Farmed insects live in conditions worse than any other farmed animal: packed boxes, water only from evaporation, cannibalism and uncleaned corpses
A study of 300 Central European insect farms found 244 with parasite infections and 81 (about 30%) carrying parasites that can infect humans, though cooking kills most of them
About 10% of cattle carry intestinal parasites, far less than farmed insects; insects seem built only for industrial farming, since free-range insects are hardly possible
Around one trillion insects are already farmed and killed per year, mostly to feed chickens, so insect farming currently supplies industrial livestock rather than replacing it
No human population eats insects as its main protein; even where they are traditional they are an extra, and people offered a choice pick a chicken leg over a roach
Cheap production makes insects economical, not sustainable; real sustainability means reducing consumption and changing modes of production
Morality is based on feelings, not facts, so Europeans who refuse bugs will not be persuaded by pragmatic arguments; the refusal is spiritual and cultural
His view of conspiracies: follow the money; eat-the-bugs is consumerism in a new shape, packaged with morality to sell cricket protein and insect snacks
About one third of all food produced is thrown away, enough to feed everyone, so anyone serious about the planet would tackle food waste before pushing new protein sources
Conclusion: insects are a valid protein source but not a nutrition revolution, and production needs major work on safety and sustainability
